meta.title: Quantum Mechanics I — Module II: The Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation
meta.subject: Quantum Mechanics I (MAT/PHY, Sem 5)

glossary.definition: Separation of variables is a method for solving a partial differential equation by looking for product solutions \(\Psi(x, t) = \psi(x)\varphi(t)\) in which each factor depends on only one variable.
glossary.example: In Equation (2.2), writing \(\Psi(x, t) = \psi(x)\varphi(t)\) splits the Schrödinger equation into a time equation and a spatial equation.

glossary.definition: The time-independent Schrödinger equation \(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + V(x)\psi = E\psi\) is the ordinary differential equation that determines the spatial wave function \(\psi(x)\) and allowed energy \(E\) when \(V(x)\) is independent of time.
glossary.example: Equation (2.5) must be solved once the potential \(V(x)\) is specified.

glossary.definition: A stationary state is a separable quantum state \(\Psi(x, t) = \psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}\) whose probability density \(|\Psi(x, t)|^2 = |\psi(x)|^2\) and all expectation values remain constant in time.
glossary.example: In Equation (2.8), the wiggle factor \(e^{-iEt/\hbar}\) cancels in \(\Psi^*\Psi\), so \(\langle x\rangle\) is constant and \(\langle p\rangle = 0\).

glossary.definition: The Hamiltonian \(H(x, p) = \frac{p^2}{2m} + V(x)\) is the classical total energy function, represented in quantum mechanics by the operator \(\hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + V(x)\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.12) writes the time-independent Schrödinger equation compactly as \(\hat{H}\psi = E\psi\).

glossary.definition: An eigenvalue is the constant multiplier \(E\) obtained when an operator acts on one of its special eigenstates \(\psi\) and returns the same function multiplied by that number, \(\hat{H}\psi = E\psi\).
glossary.example: In Equation (2.14), an energy eigenstate has variance \(\sigma_H^2 = 0\), so every energy measurement returns the eigenvalue \(E\).

glossary.definition: A linear combination is a sum of functions multiplied by constant coefficients, \(\Psi(x, t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n \psi_n(x)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\), which forms the general solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.
glossary.example: In Example 2.1, combining two stationary states with different energies \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) produces an oscillating probability density.

glossary.definition: A probability amplitude \(c_n\) is the complex coefficient of \(\psi_n(x)\) in the expansion of \(\Psi(x, t)\) whose modulus squared \(|c_n|^2\) is the probability that an energy measurement returns \(E_n\).
glossary.example: By Equations (2.19)–(2.21), the probabilities satisfy \(\sum |c_n|^2 = 1\) and give average energy \(\langle H\rangle = \sum |c_n|^2 E_n\).

glossary.definition: The infinite square well is a one-dimensional potential that is zero inside \(0 \le x \le a\) and infinite outside, confining a particle completely between rigid walls at \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.22) defines \(V(x) = 0\) for \(0 \le x \le a\) and \(V(x) = \infty\) otherwise, yielding quantized energies \(E_n = \frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}\).

glossary.definition: Boundary conditions are continuity requirements on \(\psi(x)\) and \(d\psi/dx\) at the edges of a potential region that fix integration constants and restrict allowed energies.
glossary.example: At the infinite walls \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\), continuity of \(\psi(x)\) requires \(\psi(0) = \psi(a) = 0\) in Equation (2.26).

glossary.definition: The ground state \(\psi_1(x)\) is the stationary state with the lowest allowed energy \(E_1\), whereas the higher-energy stationary states \(\psi_2, \psi_3, \dots\) are called excited states.
glossary.example: In the infinite square well, the ground state has energy \(E_1 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}\) and the \(n\)th state has \(E_n = n^2 E_1\).

glossary.definition: A node is an interior zero-crossing point where \(\psi(x) = 0\) (not counting the boundary endpoints).
glossary.example: In Figure 2.2, \(\psi_1\) has zero nodes, \(\psi_2\) has one node at \(x = a/2\), and \(\psi_n\) has \(n - 1\) nodes.

glossary.definition: A family of functions \(\{\psi_n(x)\}\) is orthonormal if different functions are orthogonal and each is normalized: \(\int \psi_m(x)^*\psi_n(x)\,dx = \delta_{mn}\), where the Kronecker delta \(\delta_{mn}\) is \(1\) for \(m=n\) and \(0\) for \(m\neq n\).
glossary.example: Equations (2.33) and (2.34) combine orthogonality and normalization of the infinite square well states.

glossary.definition: Completeness is the property that any function \(f(x)\) can be written as a linear combination \(f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n\psi_n(x)\), with coefficients \(c_n = \int \psi_n(x)^*f(x)\,dx\) extracted by Fourier's trick.
glossary.example: Equation (2.40) uses Fourier's trick to find \(c_n\) from any initial state \(\Psi(x, 0)\) in the infinite square well.

glossary.definition: A free particle is a particle subject to no forces (\(V(x) = 0\) everywhere), whose separable solutions \(\Psi_k(x, t) = Ae^{i(kx - \hbar k^2 t/2m)}\) are plane waves with momentum \(p = \hbar k\).
glossary.example: By Equation (2.100), a single free-particle plane wave is not normalizable, so a free particle cannot exist in a stationary state.

glossary.definition: A wave packet is a normalizable continuous superposition of plane waves over wave number \(k\), \(\Psi(x, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\phi(k)e^{i(kx - \hbar k^2 t/2m)}\,dk\), representing a localized particle.
glossary.example: Equation (2.101) superposes waves with a range of wave numbers \(k\) so their interference localizes the particle.

glossary.definition: The Fourier transform \(\phi(k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\Psi(x, 0)e^{-ikx}\,dx\) is the integral formula from Plancherel's theorem that finds the wave-packet amplitude \(\phi(k)\) from \(\Psi(x, 0)\).
glossary.example: In Example 2.6, Equation (2.104) transforms a rectangular state in \(x\) into \(\phi(k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi a}}\frac{\sin(ka)}{k}\).

glossary.definition: The phase velocity \(v_{\text{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k}\) is the propagation speed of individual sinusoidal ripples inside a wave packet, where \(\omega(k)\) is the dispersion relation.
glossary.example: For a free quantum particle with \(\omega = \hbar k^2/(2m)\), Equation (2.108) gives \(v_{\text{phase}} = \hbar k/(2m) = \frac{1}{2}v_{\text{classical}}\).

glossary.definition: The group velocity \(v_{\text{group}} = \frac{d\omega}{dk}\) is the speed at which the overall envelope of a narrowly peaked wave packet travels through space.
glossary.example: In Equation (2.110), a free particle has \(v_{\text{group}} = d\omega/dk = \hbar k/m = v_{\text{classical}} = 2v_{\text{phase}}\).

glossary.definition: A Hermitian operator is a linear operator equal to its own Hermitian adjoint (\(\hat{H}^\dagger = \hat{H}\)), which guarantees that the norm \(\langle\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle\) is independent of time.
glossary.example: In Zettili Equation (3.78), \(\hat{H}^\dagger = \hat{H}\) makes \(\frac{d}{dt}\langle\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle = 0\).

glossary.definition: The probability current density \(\vec{J}(\vec{r}, t) = \frac{i\hbar}{2m}(\Psi\vec{\nabla}\Psi^* - \Psi^*\vec{\nabla}\Psi)\) is the vector flux measuring the rate of probability flow per unit area.
glossary.example: For a 1D plane wave \(\psi_i(x) = Ae^{ik_1 x}\), Zettili Equation (4.21) gives \(J_{\text{incident}} = \frac{\hbar k_1}{m}|A|^2\).

glossary.definition: The continuity equation \(\frac{\partial\rho(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t} + \vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{J} = 0\) states that any local time rate of change in probability density \(\rho = \Psi^*\Psi\) is balanced by the divergence of the probability current \(\vec{J}\).
glossary.example: Zettili Equation (3.82) expresses local conservation of probability in direct analogy with charge conservation in electrodynamics.

glossary.definition: A potential step is a one-dimensional potential that is zero for \(x < 0\) and rises abruptly at \(x = 0\) to a constant plateau \(V(x) = V_0\) for \(x \ge 0\).
glossary.example: Zettili Equation (4.14) models a beam of particles incident from \(x < 0\) upon a step of height \(V_0\) at \(x = 0\).

glossary.definition: The reflection coefficient \(R = |J_{\text{reflected}}/J_{\text{incident}}|\) and transmission coefficient \(T = |J_{\text{transmitted}}/J_{\text{incident}}|\) are the fractions of an incident flux reflected and transmitted at a potential change.
glossary.example: By probability conservation in Zettili Equation (4.27), \(R + T = 1\) for a particle scattering off a potential step.

glossary.definition: A classically forbidden region is a region of space where a particle's total energy \(E\) is less than the potential energy \(V(x)\), so a classical particle cannot enter but the quantum wave function penetrates exponentially.
glossary.example: In Zettili Equation (4.34), when \(E < V_0\), the probability density in \(x \ge 0\) decays as \(P(x) = |C|^2 e^{-2k'_2 x}\).

glossary.definition: A potential barrier is a repulsive flat-topped potential of height \(V_0\) confined to a finite interval \(0 \le x \le a\), with \(V(x) = 0\) for \(x < 0\) and \(x > a\).
glossary.example: Zettili Equation (4.35) defines a rectangular barrier of width \(a\) and height \(V_0\).

glossary.definition: A transmission resonance is complete transmission (\(T = 1, R = 0\)) across a potential barrier or well when \(\sin(k_2 a) = 0\), so \(k_2 a = n\pi\) and reflected waves interfere destructively.
glossary.example: In Zettili Figure 4.4, total transmission \(T = 1\) occurs at incident energies \(E_n = V_0 + \frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}\).

glossary.definition: Tunneling is the quantum mechanical transmission of a particle through a finite potential barrier where \(E < V(x)\), emerging beyond the classical turning points with nonzero probability \(T > 0\).
glossary.example: Zettili Equations (4.65) and (4.68) give the tunneling transmission coefficient across a barrier of width \(a\) when \(E < V_0\).

cards.title: Splitting a wave function into a space shape and a time clock
cards.meaning: When the potential V(x) does not depend on time, separation of variables looks for solutions that are a simple product of a spatial shape ψ(x) and a time factor φ(t).

cards.picture: The spatial wave ψ(x) on the left multiplies the rotating complex phase φ(t) = e^{-iEt/ħ} on the right.
cards.example: A guitar string vibrates with a fixed spatial arch ψ(x) while its phase oscillates steadily in time.
cards.bridge: Dividing the Schrödinger equation by ψ(x)φ(t) puts all t-dependence on the left and all x-dependence on the right, forcing both sides to equal a constant E.

cards.title: What is the time-independent Schrödinger equation?
cards.body: Separation of variables writes \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)\varphi(t)\), turning Equation (1.1) for a time-independent potential \(V(x)\) into the time-independent Schrödinger equation, Equation (2.5).

cards.label: Derivation · §2.1
cards.title: Separation of variables and Equations (2.1)–(2.6)
cards.legend: \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)\varphi(t)\) separable wave function, \(V(x)\) time-independent potential, \(E\) separation constant.

phases.name: Product ansatz
phases.why: substitute Ψ(x,t) = ψ(x)φ(t) into Equation (2.1)

phases.name: Separate variables
phases.why: divide by ψφ so t is on the left and x is on the right

phases.name: Time equation
phases.why: equate the t-side to constant E and integrate

phases.name: Spatial equation
phases.why: equate the x-side to E to obtain Equation (2.5)

steps.note: Start with the separable product in Equation (2.2), where \(\psi\) depends only on \(x\) and \(\varphi\) only on \(t\).

ask.q: How do we isolate all \(t\)-dependence on the left and \(x\)-dependence on the right?
ask.why: Dividing through by the product ψ(x)φ(t) leaves a function of t alone on the left and a function of x alone on the right.

steps.note: Substitute the product into the Schrödinger equation (∂Ψ/∂t = ψ dφ/dt, ∂²Ψ/∂x² = φ d²ψ/dx²) and divide by \(\psi\varphi\). Equation (2.3): the left side depends only on \(t\), while the right side depends only on \(x\).

ask.q: Why must both sides of Equation (2.3) equal the same constant \(E\)?
ask.why: If the two sides were not constant, changing t would change the left side without changing the right side, breaking equality.

steps.note: Equating the left side of Equation (2.3) to the separation constant \(E\) gives Equation (2.4).

ask.q: Integrating Equation (2.4) and absorbing the constant into \(\psi\), what is \(\varphi(t)\)?
ask.why: Multiplying dφ/φ = −(iE/ħ)dt and integrating yields the exponential wiggle factor φ(t) = e^{−iEt/ħ} in Equation (2.6).

steps.note: Equation (2.6): this complex exponential is the characteristic time factor (wiggle factor).

ask.q: Setting the right side of Equation (2.3) equal to \(E\), how do we get Equation (2.5)?
ask.why: Setting −(ħ²/2m)(1/ψ)(d²ψ/dx²) + V = E and multiplying through by ψ(x) gives the time-independent Schrödinger equation.

steps.note: Equation (2.5): the time-independent Schrödinger equation determines \(\psi(x)\) and allowed energies \(E\).

cards.title: Why the wiggle factor disappears in every probability and average
cards.meaning: In a single separable state Ψ(x,t) = ψ(x)e^{-iEt/ħ}, the opposite phases e^{+iEt/ħ} and e^{-iEt/ħ} multiply to 1 inside Ψ*Ψ, freezing the probability density |ψ(x)|² in time.

cards.picture: When Ψ* and Ψ multiply, the time exponentials cancel to 1, leaving a static curve |ψ(x)|².
cards.example: Because ⟨x⟩ does not change with time, the average momentum ⟨p⟩ = m d⟨x⟩/dt is identically zero.
cards.bridge: Equation (1.36) from Module I reduces to Equation (2.9), where every expectation value ⟨Q(x,p)⟩ is constant in time.

cards.title: What is a stationary state?
cards.body: A stationary state \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}\) has constant probability density \(|\Psi|^2 = |\psi(x)|^2\), so every expectation value \(\langle Q\rangle\) is independent of time and \(\langle p\rangle = 0\).

cards.title: What is the Hamiltonian operator and a state of definite energy?
cards.body: The Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) represents total energy; a stationary state satisfies the eigenvalue equation \(\hat{H}\psi = E\psi\) with zero variance \(\sigma_H^2 = 0\), so every energy measurement gives \(E\).
cards.tex: \hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + V(x), \quad \hat{H}\psi = E\psi, \quad \sigma_H^2 = \langle H^2\rangle - \langle H\rangle^2 = E^2 - E^2 = 0

cards.title: What are the general solution and probability amplitudes?
cards.body: The general solution is a linear combination \(\Psi(x,t) = \sum c_n\psi_n(x)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\), where the probability amplitude \(c_n\) gives probability \(|c_n|^2\) of measuring energy \(E_n\).

cards.label: Example 2.1 · §2.1
cards.title: Example 2.1: Two-state superposition and oscillating |Ψ(x,t)|²
cards.legend: \(\psi_1, \psi_2\) real stationary states with energies \(E_1, E_2\), \(c_1, c_2\) real constants, \(\omega = (E_2 - E_1)/\hbar\).

phases.name: Initial superposition
phases.why: start in a linear combination of two stationary states at t = 0

phases.name: Time evolution
phases.why: tack on each state's wiggle factor exp(-iE_n t/ħ)

phases.name: Multiply Ψ*Ψ
phases.why: expand the product of Ψ*(x,t) and Ψ(x,t)

phases.name: Beat oscillation
phases.why: combine cross terms into cos[(E₂ - E₁)t/ħ]

steps.note: Start at \(t = 0\) with a linear combination of two real stationary states \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\).

ask.q: By Equation (2.17), how do we construct \(\Psi(x,t)\) from \(\Psi(x,0)\)?
ask.why: Each stationary component ψ_n(x) evolves with its own characteristic wiggle factor e^{−iE_n t/ħ}.

steps.note: Each term carries its own energy \(E_1\) or \(E_2\) in the exponent.

ask.q: What is the complex conjugate \(\Psi^*(x,t)\) for real \(c_n\) and real \(\psi_n\)?
ask.why: Since c_1, c_2, ψ_1, ψ_2 are real, taking the complex conjugate simply reverses the sign of i in the exponents.

steps.tex: |\Psi(x, t)|^2 = \left(c_1\psi_1 e^{iE_1 t/\hbar} + c_2\psi_2 e^{iE_2 t/\hbar}\right)\left(c_1\psi_1 e^{-iE_1 t/\hbar} + c_2\psi_2 e^{-iE_2 t/\hbar}\right)
steps.note: Write \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2 = \Psi^*\Psi\) to see whether the time factors cancel.

steps.tex: |\Psi(x, t)|^2 = c_1^2\psi_1^2 + c_2^2\psi_2^2 + c_1 c_2\psi_1\psi_2\left(e^{i(E_2 - E_1)t/\hbar} + e^{-i(E_2 - E_1)t/\hbar}\right)
steps.note: Diagonal terms lose their phases, while cross terms keep the energy difference \(E_2 - E_1\).

ask.q: By Euler's formula, what does \(e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}\) simplify to?
ask.why: Since e^{±iθ} = cos θ ± i sin θ, adding the two exponentials cancels the sine terms and leaves 2 cos θ.

steps.note: Unlike a single stationary state, a superposition of different energies oscillates in time.

ask.q: At what angular frequency \(\omega\) does \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2\) oscillate in Example 2.1?
ask.why: The cosine factor cos[(E_2 − E_1)t/ħ] oscillates sinusoidally with angular frequency ω = (E_2 − E_1)/ħ.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is a separable solution \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}\) called a stationary state?
options: The wave function \(\Psi(x,t)\) has no \(t\) factor
cards.why: Although Ψ(x,t) contains the time factor e^{−iEt/ħ}, it cancels in |Ψ(x,t)|² = |ψ(x)|² and in every expectation value ⟨Q⟩.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a stationary state \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}\), what is the variance \(\sigma_H^2\) of total energy?
cards.why: By Equation (2.14), ⟨H⟩ = E and ⟨H²⟩ = E², so σ_H² = ⟨H²⟩ − ⟨H⟩² = E² − E² = 0; every measurement returns E.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In Equation (2.10), the classical total energy function \(H(x,p) = \frac{p^2}{2m} + V(x)\) is called the ______.
cards.why: In classical mechanics, the total energy (kinetic plus potential) written in terms of x and p is called the Hamiltonian.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A normalized state has \(c_1 = 0.6\) and \(c_2 = 0.8\) for \(E_1 = 2\text{ eV}\), \(E_2 = 7\text{ eV}\). Find \(\langle H\rangle\).

cards.title: Standing waves trapped between two rigid walls at x = 0 and x = a
cards.meaning: An infinite square well traps a particle on 0 ≤ x ≤ a with V = 0 inside and V = ∞ outside, so ψ(x) must vanish at both walls just like a plucked guitar string.

cards.picture: Only sine waves that fit an integer number n of half-wavelengths between x = 0 and x = a can meet ψ(0) = ψ(a) = 0.
cards.example: For n = 1 there is one arch; for n = 2 there are two arches with one node at x = a/2.
cards.bridge: Restricting k to k_n = nπ/a quantizes the allowed energies to E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2ma²) in Equation (2.30).

cards.title: What is the infinite square well and its boundary conditions?
cards.body: The infinite square well traps a particle in \(0 \le x \le a\) between rigid walls where \(V(x) = \infty\); continuity of \(\psi(x)\) imposes the boundary conditions \(\psi(0) = \psi(a) = 0\).

cards.label: Derivation · §2.2
cards.title: Energy levels and stationary states of the infinite square well
cards.legend: \(a\) well width, \(k = \sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\) wave number, \(A, B\) constants, \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) quantum number.

phases.name: General solution
phases.why: solve d²ψ/dx² = -k²ψ inside 0 ≤ x ≤ a

phases.name: Left wall x = 0
phases.why: apply ψ(0) = 0 to eliminate the cosine term

phases.name: Right wall x = a
phases.why: apply ψ(a) = 0 to quantize k_n and E_n

phases.name: Normalize ψ_n
phases.why: fix A using ∫₀^a |ψ_n(x)|² dx = 1

steps.note: Equation (2.25) is the general solution to \(d^2\psi/dx^2 = -k^2\psi\) with \(k \equiv \sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\).

ask.q: Since \(\psi(0) = A\sin 0 + B\cos 0 = 0\) by Equation (2.26), what must \(B\) equal?
ask.why: Because sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1, the boundary condition ψ(0) = 0 immediately forces B = 0.

steps.note: Equation (2.27): setting \(B = 0\) leaves only the sine term.

ask.q: At \(x = a\), why do we set \(\sin(ka) = 0\) with \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) instead of \(A = 0\) or \(k = 0\)?
ask.why: Setting A = 0 or k = 0 makes ψ(x) = 0 everywhere, which cannot be normalized, and negative n merely flips the sign of A.

steps.note: Equation (2.29): the distinct non-trivial solutions require \(k_n = n\pi/a\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\).

ask.q: Using \(k_n = \sqrt{2mE_n}/\hbar = n\pi/a\), what are the allowed energies \(E_n\)?
ask.why: Squaring k_n = √(2mE_n)/ħ gives E_n = ħ²k_n²/(2m) = n²π²ħ²/(2ma²) in Equation (2.30).

steps.note: Equation (2.30): boundary conditions quantize the allowed total energies in proportion to \(n^2\).
Normalize \(\psi(x)\) using Module I Equation (1.20); the integral of \(\sin^2(n\pi x/a)\) over \([0, a]\) is \(a/2\).

ask.why: Taking A = √(2/a) gives the normalized stationary states ψ_n(x) = √(2/a) sin(nπx/a) in Equation (2.31).

cards.title: What are the ground state, excited states, and nodes?
cards.body: In the infinite square well, \(\psi_1(x)\) is the lowest-energy ground state and \(\psi_n(x)\) (\(n > 1\)) are excited states; \(\psi_n\) alternates even and odd about \(a/2\) and has \(n - 1\) nodes.
cards.tex: E_1 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}, \qquad E_n = n^2 E_1, \qquad \text{interior nodes of } \psi_n = n - 1

cards.title: What are orthonormality, completeness, and Fourier's trick?
cards.body: The stationary states \(\psi_n(x)\) are orthonormal, \(\int \psi_m^*\psi_n\,dx = \delta_{mn}\), and complete, so any state expands as \(\Psi(x,0) = \sum c_n\psi_n(x)\) with \(c_n = \int \psi_n^*\Psi(x,0)\,dx\).

ask.q: Which trigonometric identity rewrites \(2\sin A\sin B\) inside the integral?
ask.why: The product-to-sum identity 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) splits the product into two simple cosines.

ask.q: When we integrate from \(0\) to \(a\), what do \(\sin[(m - n)\pi]\) and \(\sin[(m + n)\pi]\) equal?
ask.why: Because m − n and m + n are integers, the sine of any integer multiple of π is zero.

Equation (2.33): combining \(0\) for \(m \neq n\) with \(1\) for \(m = n\) defines the orthonormal set.

ask.q: In Fourier's trick (Equation (2.36)), how do we isolate \(c_m\) from \(f(x) = \sum c_n\psi_n(x)\)?
ask.why: Multiplying both sides by ψ_m(x)* and integrating turns ∫ ψ_m* ψ_n dx into δ_mn.

steps.note: Equation (2.36): each integral \(\int \psi_m(x)^*\psi_n(x)\,dx\) inside the sum becomes \(\delta_{mn}\).

ask.q: What does the sum \(\sum c_n\delta_{mn}\) collapse to?
ask.why: The Kronecker delta δ_mn kills every term in the sum except the one with n = m, leaving c_m (Equation (2.37)).

steps.note: Equation (2.37): Fourier's trick extracts any coefficient \(c_m\) directly by integration.

cards.q: In the infinite square well of width \(a\), what is the allowed energy \(E_n\) in Equation (2.30)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.30), k_n = nπ/a gives E_n = ħ²k_n²/(2m) = n²π²ħ²/(2ma²) for n = 1, 2, 3, ….

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why are all even-numbered coefficients \(c_2, c_4, \dots\) zero in Example 2.2?
options: The potential is infinite at \(x = a/2\)
cards.why: The parabolic state Ψ(x,0) = Ax(a − x) is symmetric (even) about the center x = a/2, whereas ψ_n for even n is odd about x = a/2, so their product integrates to zero.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many interior nodes (zero-crossings excluding endpoints) does the state \(\psi_4(x)\) have?
cards.why: By Property 2 in Section 2.2, the nth stationary state ψ_n(x) has n − 1 interior nodes, so ψ_4(x) has 4 − 1 = 3 nodes.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A set of wave functions that are both mutually orthogonal and normalized is called ______.
cards.why: By Equation (2.33), ∫ ψ_m(x)* ψ_n(x) dx = δ_mn combines orthogonality (m ≠ n) and normalization (m = n) into orthonormality.

cards.title: Why a free particle must be a localized wave packet, not a single plane wave
cards.meaning: A single free-particle plane wave Ae^{i(kx - ωt)} has constant modulus |A|² from −∞ to +∞ and cannot be normalized; superposing a continuous range of k builds a normalizable wave packet.
cards.picture: Compare the unnormalizable infinite wave on top with the localized wave packet built by interference below.
cards.example: Adding waves of nearby wave numbers k cancels the tails far away and builds a localized hump.
cards.bridge: Equation (2.101) replaces the discrete sum over n with a continuous integral over k weighted by φ(k).

cards.title: What is a free particle's separable solution?
cards.body: A free particle moves where \(V(x) = 0\) everywhere; its separable plane-wave solutions \(\Psi_k(x,t) = Ae^{i(kx - \hbar k^2 t/2m)}\) have infinite integral and are non-normalizable.
cards.tex: \Psi_k(x, t) = Ae^{i\left(kx - \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m}t\right)}, \quad p = \hbar k, \quad v_{\text{quantum}} = \frac{\hbar|k|}{2m} = \sqrt{\frac{E}{2m}} = \frac{1}{2}v_{\text{classical}}

cards.title: What are a wave packet and its Fourier transform φ(k)?
cards.body: A wave packet is a normalizable integral superposition of plane waves over wave number \(k\) (Equation (2.101)), where Plancherel's theorem gives the Fourier transform \(\phi(k)\) from \(\Psi(x,0)\).

ask.why: Dividing by 2a and taking the positive square root gives A = 1/√(2a).

steps.note: The normalized height of the initial step wave function is \(A = 1/\sqrt{2a}\).

ask.q: By Equation (2.104), which integral gives the momentum amplitude \(\phi(k)\)?
ask.why: Plugging Ψ(x,0) = 1/√(2a) on (−a, a) into Equation (2.104) restricts the limits to −a and a.

Antiderivative \(\frac{e^{-ikx}}{-ik}\) evaluated from \(-a\) to \(a\) forms \(\frac{e^{ika} - e^{-ika}}{2i}\).

ask.q: Using Euler's identity \(\frac{e^{ika} - e^{-ika}}{2i} = \sin(ka)\), what is \(\phi(k)\)?
ask.why: Replacing the bracket by sin(ka) gives φ(k) = (1/√(πa))(sin(ka)/k) (Figure 2.9b).

steps.note: Small \(a\) gives narrow \(\Psi(x,0)\) and broad \(\phi(k)\), illustrating the uncertainty principle.

ask.q: How do we obtain \(\Psi(x,t)\) in Equation (2.105) from \(\phi(k)\)?
ask.why: Plugging φ(k) back into Equation (2.101) with √(2π)√(πa) = π√(2a) gives Equation (2.105).

cards.title: Ripples inside an envelope: phase velocity vs group velocity
cards.meaning: A wave packet consists of rapid sinusoidal ripples moving at the phase velocity v_p = ω/k inside a smooth outer envelope that travels at the group velocity v_g = dω/dk.
cards.picture: Look at Figure 2.10: the outer dashed envelope moves at v_g = dω/dk while the inner ripples move at v_p = ω/k.
cards.example: When you toss a rock into a pond, individual ripples travel twice as fast as the expanding ring of waves; for a quantum free particle, the group travels twice as fast as the ripples.
cards.bridge: Because ω = ħk²/(2m), differentiating gives v_group = dω/dk = ħk/m = v_classical = 2v_phase.

cards.title: What are phase velocity and group velocity?
cards.body: Phase velocity \(v_{\text{phase}} = \omega/k\) is the speed of individual ripples, whereas group velocity \(v_{\text{group}} = d\omega/dk\) is the envelope speed matching \(v_{\text{classical}} = 2v_{\text{phase}}\).
cards.tex: v_{\text{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{\hbar k}{2m}, \qquad v_{\text{group}} = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \frac{\hbar k}{m}, \qquad v_{\text{classical}} = v_{\text{group}} = 2v_{\text{phase}}

ask.q: In Equation (2.107), at what speed does the envelope function of \((x - \omega'_0 t)\) travel?
ask.why: Any function of (x − vt) propagates without changing shape at speed v, so the envelope travels at v_group = ω'₀ = dω/dk.

ask.q: For a free particle with \(\omega = \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m}\), what is \(v_{\text{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k}\)?
ask.why: Dividing ω = ħk²/(2m) by k gives v_phase = ħk/(2m).

ask.q: Differentiating \(\omega = \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m}\) with respect to \(k\), what is \(v_{\text{group}} = \frac{d\omega}{dk}\)?
ask.why: Taking d/dk of ħk²/(2m) brings down a factor of 2, giving v_group = ħk/m = 2v_phase = v_classical (Equation (2.110)).

steps.note: Equation (2.110): since \(p = \hbar k\), \(v_{\text{group}} = p/m = v_{\text{classical}} = 2v_{\text{phase}}\), resolving the speed paradox.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why can a free particle NOT exist in a stationary state \(\Psi_k(x,t)\)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.100), ∫_{-∞}^{+∞} |Ψ_k|² dx = |A|²(∞), so a single separable plane wave cannot be normalized.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which theorem provides the Fourier transform \(\phi(k)\) from \(\Psi(x,0)\) in Equations (2.103)–(2.104)?
cards.why: Plancherel's theorem (Equation (2.103)) gives the symmetric Fourier transform pair linking f(x) and F(k).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For a free-particle wave packet, what is the ratio \(v_{\text{group}} / v_{\text{phase}}\)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.110), v_group = ħk/m and v_phase = ħk/(2m), so v_group / v_phase = 2.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In a wave packet, the formula for \(\omega\) as a function of \(k\) is called the ______ relation.
cards.why: As defined in Section 2.4 (page 59), the formula relating angular frequency ω to wave number k is the dispersion relation.

cards.title: Why probability cannot vanish at one point without flowing out as a current
cards.meaning: Just as electric charge is locally conserved via ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0, any decrease of probability density ρ = Ψ*Ψ inside a region must equal the outward flow of probability current J.

(3.82): ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J⃗ = 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: When probability density ρ inside the box drops (∂ρ/∂t < 0), probability current density J⃗ flows outward (∇·J⃗ > 0).
cards.example: In electrodynamics, charge leaving a volume creates an electric current; in quantum mechanics, probability leaving a volume creates a probability current.
cards.bridge: Combining the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (3.79) and its conjugate (3.80) produces the continuity equation (3.82).

cards.label: 01 · Zettili §3.6.4
cards.title: What keeps the norm ⟨Ψ(t)|Ψ(t)⟩ constant in time?
cards.body: Because the Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator (\(\hat{H}^\dagger = \hat{H}\)), the time derivative of the norm \(\langle\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle\) vanishes (Zettili Equation (3.78)), conserving total probability.

cards.label: 02 · Zettili §3.6.4
cards.title: What are probability current density and the continuity equation?
cards.body: Probability current density \(\vec{J}\) is the probability flux (Zettili Equation (3.83)); with \(\rho = \Psi^*\Psi\), it obeys the continuity equation \(\partial\rho/\partial t + \vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{J} = 0\).

cards.label: Derivation · Zettili §3.6.4
cards.title: Continuity equation and probability current (Zettili Equations (3.79)–(3.83))
cards.legend: \(\Psi(\vec{r},t)\) wave function, \(\rho(\vec{r},t) = \Psi^*\Psi\) probability density, \(\vec{J}(\vec{r},t)\) probability current density.

phases.why: divide by iħ and identify ρ(r⃗,t) = Ψ*Ψ

phases.name: Continuity equation

steps.note: Start with Zettili Equation (3.79) in the position representation.
Zettili Equation (3.80): take the complex conjugate of Equation (3.79).

ask.q: How do we combine Equations (3.79) and (3.80) to eliminate \(\hat{V}(\vec{r},t)\)?
ask.why: Multiplying (3.79) by Ψ*(r⃗,t) and (3.80) by Ψ(r⃗,t) and subtracting cancels the potential term V̂Ψ*Ψ and forms ∂(Ψ*Ψ)/∂t.

steps.tex: i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left[\Psi^*(\vec{r}, t)\Psi(\vec{r}, t)\right] = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left[\Psi^*(\vec{r}, t)\nabla^2\Psi(\vec{r}, t) - \Psi\nabla^2\Psi^*\right]
steps.note: Zettili Equation (3.81): subtracting the two equations combines the time derivatives via the product rule.

ask.q: Defining \(\rho(\vec{r},t) = \Psi^*(\vec{r},t)\Psi(\vec{r},t)\), how do we isolate \(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}\)?
ask.why: Dividing by iħ (and using −1/i = +i) isolates ∂ρ/∂t on the left-hand side.

ask.q: In Zettili Equation (3.83), what vector is defined as \(\frac{i\hbar}{2m}(\Psi\vec{\nabla}\Psi^* - \Psi^*\vec{\nabla}\Psi)\)?
ask.why: Zettili Equation (3.83) defines J⃗(r⃗,t) = (iħ/2m)(Ψ∇Ψ* − Ψ*∇Ψ) as the probability current density.

steps.note: Substitute the probability current density \(\vec{J}(\vec{r}, t)\) from Equation (3.83).

ask.q: Moving \(-\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{J}\) to the left side gives which conservation law (Equation (3.82))?
ask.why: Adding ∇·J⃗ to both sides yields Zettili Equation (3.82), the continuity equation for conservation of probability.

steps.note: Zettili Equation (3.82): the equation of continuity expresses local conservation of probability.

cards.label: Zettili Eqs. (3.83)–(3.85)
cards.title: 1D Probability Current and the Density Operator ρ̂(t)
cards.tex: J(x, t) = \frac{i\hbar}{2m}\left(\Psi\frac{\partial\Psi^*}{\partial x} - \Psi^*\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial x}\right), \qquad \hat{\rho}(t) = |\Psi(t)\rangle\langle\Psi(t)| = \hat{U}(t, t_0)\hat{\rho}(t_0)\hat{U}^\dagger(t, t_0)
cards.body: In 1D, \(\vec{\nabla}\) becomes \(\partial/\partial x\); if \(\Psi(x,t)\) is purely real (\(\Psi^* = \Psi\)), \(J(x,t) = 0\). In operator form (Zettili Equations (3.84)–(3.85)), the density operator \(\hat{\rho}(t) = |\Psi(t)\rangle\langle\Psi(t)|\) evolves via \(\hat{U}(t,t_0)\).

cards.q: In Zettili Section 3.6.4, why is the norm \(\langle\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle\) independent of time?
cards.why: By Zettili Equations (3.76)–(3.78), Ĥ† = Ĥ causes the two terms in d⟨Ψ(t)|Ψ(t)⟩/dt to cancel with opposite signs (i/ħ − i/ħ) = 0.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which expression defines the probability current density \(\vec{J}(\vec{r},t)\) in Zettili Equation (3.83)?
cards.why: Zettili Equation (3.83) defines the probability current density (particle density flux) as J⃗(r⃗,t) = (iħ/2m)(Ψ∇Ψ* − Ψ*∇Ψ).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By analogy with electrodynamics, \(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{J} = 0\) is called the equation of ______.
cards.why: Zettili Equation (3.82) is the continuity equation, expressing the local conservation of probability.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the probability current density \(\vec{J}\) of any purely real wave function \(\Psi^* = \Psi\)?
cards.why: When Ψ* = Ψ, the two terms Ψ∇Ψ* and Ψ*∇Ψ in Zettili Equation (3.83) are identical, so their difference is zero.

cards.label: 01 · Zettili §4.4(a)
cards.title: What are the potential step and coefficients R and T for E > V₀?
cards.body: A potential step jumps from \(V=0\) (\(x<0\)) to \(V_0\) (\(x\ge 0\)); the reflection and transmission coefficients \(R\) and \(T\) are the reflected and transmitted current ratios, with \(R + T = 1\).
cards.tex: R = \left|\frac{J_{\text{reflected}}}{J_{\text{incident}}}\right| = \frac{|B|^2}{|A|^2} = \frac{(k_1 - k_2)^2}{(k_1 + k_2)^2}, \qquad T = \left|\frac{J_{\text{transmitted}}}{J_{\text{incident}}}\right| = \frac{k_2|C|^2}{k_1|A|^2} = \frac{4k_1 k_2}{(k_1 + k_2)^2}

cards.label: Derivation · Zettili §4.4(a)
cards.title: Reflection and transmission at a potential step for E > V₀ (Eqs. (4.20)–(4.27))
cards.legend: \(k_1 = \sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\), \(k_2 = \sqrt{2m(E-V_0)}/\hbar\), \(A, B, C\) incident, reflected, transmitted amplitudes, \(\mathcal{K} = k_2/k_1\).

objects.text: At x = 0: A + B = C, k₁(A − B) = k₂C
objects.name: match0

phases.name: Current ratios
phases.why: compute J_inc, J_ref, J_tr to get R and T in Equation (4.23)

phases.name: Continuity at x = 0
phases.why: match ψ₁(0) = ψ₂(0) and dψ₁(0)/dx = dψ₂(0)/dx

phases.name: Solve for B & C
phases.why: express B and C in terms of A in Equation (4.26)

phases.name: Find R and T
phases.why: substitute B/A and C/A into Equation (4.23)

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.21): for \(\psi_i(x) = Ae^{ik_1 x}\), the incident current density is \(\frac{\hbar k_1}{m}|A|^2\).

ask.q: Since \(J_{\text{transmitted}} = \frac{\hbar k_2}{m}|C|^2\), what is \(T = \left|\frac{J_{\text{transmitted}}}{J_{\text{incident}}}\right|\)?
ask.why: Because Regions I and II have different wave numbers k₁ and k₂, the flux ratio T carries the speed factor k₂/k₁ (Zettili Equation (4.23)).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.23): similarly \(R = |J_{\text{reflected}}/J_{\text{incident}}| = |B|^2/|A|^2\).

ask.q: With \(\psi_1 = Ae^{ik_1 x} + Be^{-ik_1 x}\) and \(\psi_2 = Ce^{ik_2 x}\), what does \(\psi_1(0) = \psi_2(0)\) give?
ask.why: Setting x = 0 makes every exponential equal 1, yielding A + B = C in Zettili Equation (4.25).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.25a): continuity of \(\psi(x)\) at \(x = 0\).
Zettili Equation (4.25b): continuity of \(d\psi/dx\) at \(x = 0\) after canceling \(i\).

ask.q: Adding \(k_1(A + B) = k_1 C\) and \(k_1(A - B) = k_2 C\), what is \(C\) in terms of \(A\)?
ask.why: Adding the two equations eliminates B and gives 2k₁A = (k₁ + k₂)C, so C = [2k₁/(k₁ + k₂)]A (Zettili Equation (4.26)).

move.label: Solve system for B and C

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.26): \(B = \frac{k_1 - k_2}{k_1 + k_2}A\) and \(C = \frac{2k_1}{k_1 + k_2}A\).

ask.q: Substituting \(B\) and \(C\) into Equation (4.23), what is \(R + T\)?
ask.why: Since (k₁ − k₂)² + 4k₁k₂ = (k₁ + k₂)², the reflection and transmission coefficients sum to 1.

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.27): \(R = \frac{(1 - \mathcal{K})^2}{(1 + \mathcal{K})^2}\) and \(T = \frac{4k_1 k_2}{(k_1 + k_2)^2} = \frac{4\mathcal{K}}{(1 + \mathcal{K})^2}\) with \(\mathcal{K} = \sqrt{1 - V_0/E}\).

cards.label: 02 · Zettili §4.4(b)
cards.title: What happens at a potential step when E < V₀?
cards.body: When \(E < V_0\) at a potential step, the region \(x \ge 0\) is a classically forbidden region where \(\psi_2(x) = Ce^{-k'_2 x}\) decays exponentially, giving \(J_{\text{transmitted}} = 0\) and \(R = 1\).

cards.label: Derivation · Zettili §4.4(b)
cards.title: Total reflection and penetration for E < V₀ (Zettili Equations (4.28)–(4.34))
cards.legend: \(k'_2 = \sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}/\hbar\) decay constant in \(x \ge 0\), \(\psi_t(x) = Ce^{-k'_2 x}\), \(P(x) = |\psi_t(x)|^2\).

phases.name: Region II solution
phases.why: solve Equation (4.28) for x ≥ 0 and keep the finite decaying term

phases.name: Transmitted flux
phases.why: show J_transmitted = 0 in Equation (4.31)

phases.name: Match at x = 0
phases.why: find B and C in terms of A in Equation (4.32)

phases.name: Total reflection & P(x)
phases.why: verify R = 1 and find P(x) = |ψ_t(x)|² in Equations (4.33)–(4.34)

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.29) solves \((d^2/dx^2 - {k'_2}^2)\psi_2(x) = 0\) with \({k'_2}^2 = 2m(V_0 - E)/\hbar^2\).

ask.q: Why must the constant \(D\) equal zero in Zettili Equation (4.29)?
ask.why: Since the wave function must remain finite everywhere and e^{k'₂x} blows up as x → ∞, we must set D = 0.

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.31): up to an overall phase, \(\psi_t(x) = Ce^{-k'_2 x}\) has identical terms that cancel to \(0\).

ask.q: Matching \(\psi_1(0) = \psi_2(0)\) and \(\psi'_1(0) = \psi'_2(0)\) gives \(A+B=C\) and \(ik_1(A-B) = -k'_2 C\). What is \(B\)?
ask.why: Dividing the derivative condition by ik₁ gives A − B = (ik'₂/k₁)C, yielding B = [(k₁ − ik'₂)/(k₁ + ik'₂)]A in Equation (4.32).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.32): simultaneously \(C = \frac{2k_1}{k_1 + ik'_2}A\).

ask.q: What is the modulus squared \(|k_1 - ik'_2|^2\) in the numerator of \(R = |B|^2/|A|^2\)?
ask.why: For any complex number x ± iy, the modulus squared is x² + y², so both numerator and denominator equal k₁² + k'₂².

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.33): we have total reflection (\(R = 1\)), just as in classical mechanics.

ask.q: Using \(C = \frac{2k_1}{k_1 + ik'_2}A\), what is the penetration probability density \(P(x) = |\psi_t(x)|^2\) for \(x > 0\)?
ask.why: Squaring the modulus of ψ_t(x) = Ce^{−k'₂x} gives Zettili Equation (4.34), showing nonzero penetration near x = 0.

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.34): unlike the classical case, there is a nonzero probability of finding the particle in \(x > 0\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Zettili Section 4.4, why must \(d\psi/dx\) be continuous across the potential step at \(x = 0\)?
cards.why: As stated on page 223 of Zettili, continuity of linear momentum P̂ψ(x) = −iħ dψ(x)/dx requires dψ/dx to be continuous at x = 0.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When \(E < V_0\) at a potential step, what are the reflection coefficient \(R\) and probability density \(P(x)\) for \(x > 0\)?
cards.why: By Zettili Equations (4.33) and (4.34), there is total reflection (R = 1) with J_transmitted = 0, yet P(x) = |C|²e^{−2k'₂x} penetrates exponentially into x > 0.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A particle hits a potential step with \(E = \frac{4}{3}V_0\), so \(\mathcal{K} = \sqrt{1 - V_0/E} = 0.5\). Find \(R\) to two decimals.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: When \(E < V_0\), the region \(x > 0\) where classical kinetic energy would be negative is classically ______.
cards.why: In Zettili Section 4.4(b) (page 224), the region x > 0 where E < V₀ is called the classically forbidden region.

cards.title: Three regions across a finite barrier of width a (0 ≤ x ≤ a)
cards.meaning: A potential barrier has V(x) = V₀ only inside Region II (0 ≤ x ≤ a) and V(x) = 0 in Region I (x < 0) and Region III (x > a), allowing an outgoing wave Ee^{ik₁x} beyond x = a.

cards.label: 01 · Zettili §4.5.1
cards.title: What are a potential barrier for E > V₀ and transmission resonances?
cards.body: A potential barrier has height \(V_0\) across \(0 \le x \le a\); for \(E > V_0\), wave interference causes partial reflection except at transmission resonances \(k_2 a = n\pi\) where \(T = 1\).

cards.label: Derivation · Zettili §4.5.1
cards.title: Barrier transmission coefficient for E > V₀ and resonances (Eqs. (4.37)–(4.44))

objects.text: Match ψ and dψ/dx at x = 0 and x = a
objects.name: bc0a

phases.name: Boundary conditions
phases.why: match ψ and dψ/dx at x = 0 and x = a to get Equation (4.41)

phases.name: Transmission T
phases.why: compute T = |E|²/|A|² in Zettili Equation (4.42)

phases.name: Dimensionless form
phases.why: introduce ε = E/V₀ and λ = a√(2mV₀)/ħ in Equation (4.44)

phases.name: Resonance energies
phases.why: set sin(k₂a) = 0 so T = 1 at k₂a = nπ

steps.tex: E = 4k_1 k_2 Ae^{-ik_1 a}\left[4k_1 k_2\cos(k_2 a) - 2i\left(k_1^2 + k_2^2\right)\sin(k_2 a)\right]^{-1}
steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.41): solving the continuity equations (4.39)–(4.40) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\) for \(E\).

ask.q: In Region III (\(x \ge a\)), the wave speed is \(\hbar k_1/m\) (same as Region I). What is \(T\)?
ask.why: Since both Region I and Region III have V = 0 and wave number k₁, the k₁ factors cancel in T = (k₁|E|²)/(k₁|A|²) = |E|²/|A|².

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.42a): taking the modulus squared of Equation (4.41) and simplifying \(\cos^2(k_2 a) + \sin^2(k_2 a) = 1\).

ask.q: Using \(k_1^2 = 2mE/\hbar^2\) and \(k_2^2 = 2m(E - V_0)/\hbar^2\), what is \(\left(\frac{k_1^2 - k_2^2}{k_1 k_2}\right)^2\) in Equation (4.43)?
ask.why: The difference k₁² − k₂² is 2mV₀/ħ² and the product k₁²k₂² is (2m/ħ²)²E(E − V₀), giving V₀²/[E(E − V₀)] (Equation (4.43)).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.44): dimensionless transmission coefficient for \(E > V_0\).

ask.q: When does total transmission (\(T = 1\), resonance) occur in Equation (4.42) or (4.44)?
ask.why: Whenever sin(k₂a) = sin(λ√(ε − 1)) = 0, the second term in the bracket vanishes and T = [1 + 0]⁻¹ = 1.

steps.note: Constructive interference gives total transmission \(T = 1\) when \(k_2 a = n\pi\) (\(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)).

ask.q: Solving \(k_2^2 a^2 = \frac{2m(E_n - V_0)a^2}{\hbar^2} = n^2\pi^2\), what are the resonance energies \(E_n\)?
ask.why: As shown on page 226 of Zettili, the transmission maxima occur at E_n = V₀ + n²π²ħ²/(2ma²), shifted by V₀ from the infinite square well levels.

steps.note: Total transmission \(T(\varepsilon_n) = 1\) occurs at these resonance energies (observed in the Ramsauer–Townsend effect).

cards.title: How a wave decays inside a barrier (E < V₀) and emerges on the other side
cards.meaning: When E < V₀, the wave function does not drop to zero instantly inside 0 ≤ x ≤ a; it decays exponentially across the barrier and joins onto a smaller oscillating wave for x ≥ a.

cards.example: Alpha particles escape atomic nuclei and electrons cross thin oxide layers in tunnel diodes by quantum tunneling.
cards.bridge: Replacing sin(k₂a) with i sinh(k₂a) when E < V₀ gives the finite tunneling transmission coefficient in Zettili Equations (4.62)–(4.68).

cards.label: 02 · Zettili §4.5.2
cards.title: What is quantum tunneling (E < V₀) across a potential barrier?
cards.body: Quantum tunneling is the passage of a particle with \(E < V_0\) through a finite barrier \(0 \le x \le a\), yielding a nonzero transmission coefficient \(T > 0\) in region \(x \ge a\).
cards.tex: \psi_2(x) = Ce^{k_2 x} + De^{-k_2 x}, \qquad T = \left[1 + \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{k_1^2 + k_2^2}{k_1 k_2}\right)^2\sinh^2(k_2 a)\right]^{-1}, \quad k_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}}{\hbar}

cards.label: Derivation · Zettili §4.5.2
cards.title: Tunneling transmission coefficient and wide-barrier limit (Eqs. (4.58)–(4.68))

phases.name: Modulus squared |E/A|²
phases.why: take |E/A|² from Equation (4.58) to get Equation (4.60)

phases.name: Hyperbolic identity
phases.why: use cosh²(k₂a) = 1 + sinh²(k₂a) to reach Equation (4.62)

phases.name: Energy form
phases.why: use Equation (4.63) to write T in terms of E and V₀

phases.name: Opaque barrier limit
phases.why: approximate sinh(k₂a) ≃ ½e^{k₂a} for k₂a ≫ 1 in Equation (4.68)

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.60): take \(T = |E|^2/|A|^2\) from the transmitted amplitude ratio in Equation (4.58).

ask.q: Which hyperbolic identity rewrites \(\cosh^2(k_2 a)\) so we can combine the \(\sinh^2(k_2 a)\) terms?
ask.why: Since cosh²(k₂a) − sinh²(k₂a) = 1, replacing cosh²(k₂a) by 1 + sinh²(k₂a) turns 4 + ((k₂² − k₁²)/(k₁k₂))² into ((k₁² + k₂²)/(k₁k₂))².

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.62): since \(\sinh^2(k_2 a) > 0\) for \(a > 0\), \(T\) is finite and nonzero.

ask.q: With \(k_1^2 = 2mE/\hbar^2\) and \(k_2^2 = 2m(V_0 - E)/\hbar^2\), what is \(\left(\frac{k_1^2 + k_2^2}{k_1 k_2}\right)^2\) in Equation (4.63)?
ask.why: Adding k₁² + k₂² cancels E and leaves 2mV₀/ħ², so squaring ((k₁² + k₂²)/(k₁k₂)) gives V₀²/[E(V₀ − E)] (Zettili Equation (4.63)).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.65): in dimensionless variables \(\varepsilon = E/V_0\), \(T = [1 + \frac{1}{4\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)}\sinh^2(\lambda\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon})]^{-1}\).

ask.q: When \(E \ll V_0\) so \(k_2 a = \lambda\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon} \gg 1\), how do we approximate \(\sinh(k_2 a)\)?
ask.why: For large argument u ≫ 1, e^{−u} is negligible compared to e^u, so sinh u = (e^u − e^{−u})/2 ≃ ½e^u.

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.68a): drop the negligible \(1\) compared to the large exponential in the bracket.

ask.q: Replacing \(\varepsilon = E/V_0\) and \(\lambda\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon} = (a/\hbar)\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}\), what is \(T\) in Equation (4.68)?
ask.why: Substituting ε = E/V₀ and 2λ√(1 − ε) = (2a/ħ)√(2m(V₀ − E)) gives Zettili Equation (4.68).

steps.note: Zettili Equation (4.68): tunneling probability decays exponentially with barrier width \(a\) and \(\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}\).

cards.label: Zettili §4.5.3 · Eqs. (4.69)–(4.71)
cards.title: Smooth Potential Barrier and WKB Tunneling Formula
cards.tex: T_i \sim \exp\left[-\frac{2\Delta x_i}{\hbar}\sqrt{2m(V(x_i) - E)}\right] \implies T \sim \exp\left\{-\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_{x_1}^{x_2} dx\,\sqrt{2m\left[V(x) - E\right]}\right\}
cards.body: For a smoothly varying barrier \(V(x) > E\) between classical turning points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) (Figure 4.5), slicing \([x_1, x_2]\) into thin square barriers \(\Delta x_i\) and multiplying \(\prod_i T_i\) yields Zettili Equation (4.69).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Zettili Equation (4.48) for \(E < V_0\), why do we keep BOTH \(Ce^{k_2 x}\) and \(De^{-k_2 x}\) inside \(0 < x < a\)?
options: Because the barrier width \(0 < x < a\) is finite
Because \(k_2\) is zero inside the barrier
cards.why: Unlike the potential step which extends to x → ∞, the barrier region 0 < x < a has finite width a, so e^{k₂x} remains finite and cannot be dropped.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Zettili Section 4.5.2 (page 229), what happens to \(R\) and \(T\) for \(E < V_0\) in the classical limit \(\hbar \to 0\)?
cards.why: As ħ → 0, λ = a√(2mV₀)/ħ → ∞, so sinh(λ√(1 − ε)) → ∞ in Zettili Equations (4.66)–(4.67), recovering the classical result T → 0 and R → 1.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In Zettili Section 4.5.1, total transmission maxima (\(T = 1\)) when \(k_2 a = n\pi\) are called ______.
cards.why: On page 226 of Zettili, the maxima where T = 1 at k₂a = nπ are called resonances, arising from constructive interference.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In Zettili Equation (4.46), as \(E \to V_0\) (\(\varepsilon \to 1\)) with \(\frac{ma^2 V_0}{2\hbar^2} = 3\), what is \(T\)?
cards.why: By Zettili Equation (4.46), in the limit ε → 1 we have T = [1 + ma²V₀/(2ħ²)]⁻¹ = (1 + 3)⁻¹ = 1/4 = 0.25.
